οὐ μὴν οὐδ᾿ ἀλόγως ἐκινήθησαν οἱ νομίσαντες Ἱπποκράτους εἶναι καὶ ταῦτα· κατὰ γὰρ τὴν ἐκείνου προαίρεσιν ἡ διάνοια τῶν γεγραμμένων 733 ἐστὶν, ὡς ὑπονοῆσαι μαθητὴν αὐτοῦ τινα γεγραφέναι. πολλὰ δὲ ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ τὴν λέξιν ἄμεμπτον ἔχει μετὰ τῆς διανοίας, ὡς ὑπονοῆσαι πάλιν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ἱπποκράτους αὐτὰ γεγράφθαι, παρασκευαζομένου συνθεῖναι βιβλίον, ὡς ὑπέσχετο κατὰ αὐτὸ τὸ περὶ διαίτης ὀξέων, ἐν ᾧ κατὰ μέρος ἑκάστου τῶν ὀξέων νοσημάτων τὴν θεραπείαν διδάξει. καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ ἄλλας ἔστι ῥήσεις εὑρεῖν ἐν τῷ προκειμένῳ βιβλίῳ, φανερῶς οὐκ οὔσας ἀξίας Ἱπποκράτους, ὡς ὑπονοῆσαι παρεγγεγράφθαι τοῖς γνησίοις, ὥσπερ καὶ κατὰ τοὺς ἀφορισμοὺς ἐφάνησαν ἔνιοι τοιοῦτοι πρὸς τοῖς τελευταίοις μέρεσι τοῦ βιβλίου. τῷ γὰρ ἐν μνήμῃ πολλοῖς εἶναι τὰ πρῶτα τῶν συγγραμμάτων, οἱ παρεγγράφοντες εἰς τὰ τελευταῖα παρεγγράφουσι· τοῦτο γοῦν αὐτὸ καὶ κατὰ τὸ περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ τρωμάτων ἐφάνη γεγονὸς, ἔτι δὲ κατὰ τὸ δεύτερον τῶν ἐπιδημιῶν. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ κατὰ τὸ νῦν ἡμῖν προκείμενον βιβλίον ἔστιν εὑρεῖν παρεγκείμενα καὶ μᾶλλον ἔτι πρὸς τοῖς τελευταίοις.

Rendering A (fable-5-1)

Yet neither were those who held that these parts too are Hippocrates' moved without reason; for the thought of what has been written 733 accords with that man's doctrinal position, so that one would suspect that some pupil of his wrote it. Many things in them, moreover, have the diction too faultless, along with the thought, so that one would suspect in turn that they were written by Hippocrates himself as he was preparing to compose a book, as he promised in the very work On Regimen in Acute Diseases, in which he would teach in detail the treatment of each of the acute diseases. And indeed one can also find other passages in the book before us that are manifestly not worthy of Hippocrates, so that one would suspect they have been interpolated among the genuine ones, just as in the Aphorisms too some such passages appeared toward the final parts of the book. For because the first parts of treatises are in the memory of many, those who interpolate insert their interpolations into the last parts; at any rate this very thing appeared to have happened in the work On Wounds in the Head, and further in the second book of the Epidemics. Likewise in the book now before us too one can find inserted material, and still more toward the end.

Yet those who held that these parts too are by Hippocrates were not moved without reason either; for the sense of what is written 733 accords with his approach, so that one might suspect that some pupil of his wrote it. Moreover, one can also find other passages in the present book that are manifestly not worthy of Hippocrates, so that one might suspect that they have been interpolated among the genuine ones, just as in the Aphorisms too some such passages appeared towards the last parts of the book. Since, then, there are, as one might say, four kinds in it — the kind worthy of Hippocrates both 734 in diction and in thought, the kind worthy in one respect only, either the diction or the thought, and some passages worthy in neither respect — we shall indicate this very point in the case of each of the passages taken in hand for exegesis. "Causus arises whenever the small veins, having been dried up in the summer season, draw to themselves pungent and bilious ichors." By "summer season" he has meant the hot and dry one, whether it be at the end of spring, or at the beginning of summer, or in its middle or final parts, or at the beginning of autumn.

δέδεικται δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ὑπομνήμασι τῶν ἐπιδημιῶν ἡ τοῦ περιέχοντος ἀέρος κρᾶσις ἑαυτῇ συμμεταβάλλουσα τὴν τοῦ σώματος διάθεσιν, ἡ μὲν ξηρὰ πρὸς τὸ ξηρότερον, ἡ δ᾿ ὑγρὰ πρὸς τὸ ὑγρότερον· ἐπιδέδεικται δὲ καὶ ὅτι τὴν κατὰ 735 φύσιν κρᾶσιν σύμμετρος ὥρα φυλάττει, τῶν ἄλλων δηλονότι πάντων ὡσαύτως ἐχόντων, ὅσα κατὰ τὴν ὅλην δίαιταν οἱ ἄνθρωποι πράττουσιν. ἐπιδέδεικται δὲ καὶ ὅτι τῆς κατὰ φύσιν τε καὶ συμμέτρου καταστάσεως ἐξιστάμενον τὸ σῶμα, καθότι ἂν ἐξίστηταί τε καὶ μεταβέβληται, κατὰ τοῦτο καὶ τῆς οἰκείας ἐπικουρίας δεῖται, ξηραινόμενον μὲν ὑγραίνεσθαι, ὑγραινόμενον δὲ ξηραίνεσθαι, θερμαινόμενον δὲ ψύχεσθαι, ψυχόμενον δὲ θερμαίνεσθαι. ὅτε οὖν κατά τινα περίστασιν πραγμάτων, ὧν αὐτὸς ἐρεῖ παραδείγματα, συμβῇ τινα ξηρανθῆναι φλεβία καθ᾿ ὁτιοῦν μέρος τοῦ σώματος, ἐπισπᾶται ταῦτα τὰς ἐκ τῶν πλησιαζόντων μορίων ὑγρότητας.

It has been shown in the commentaries on the Epidemics that the mixture of the surrounding air changes the condition of the body along with itself, the dry mixture toward the drier, the moist toward the moister; and it has also been demonstrated that a well-proportioned season preserves the 735 natural mixture, provided of course that all the other things are the same, namely all that human beings do in their regimen as a whole. And it has also been demonstrated that the body, when it departs from its natural and proportionate constitution, in whatever respect it departs and has been changed, in that same respect also requires the appropriate assistance: when it is being dried, to be moistened; when being moistened, to be dried; when being heated, to be cooled; when being cooled, to be heated. When, therefore, through some circumstance of affairs, of which he himself will give examples, it happens that certain small veins are dried in any part whatsoever of the body, these draw to themselves the moistures from the neighbouring parts.

Rendering B (opus-5-5) · unsure: ἑαυτῇ συμμεταβάλλουσα

It has been shown in the commentaries on the Epidemics that the mixture of the surrounding air changes the condition of the body along with itself, the dry mixture towards the drier, the moist towards the moister. It has also been demonstrated that a well-proportioned season preserves the 735 natural mixture, provided, of course, that all the other things people do in the whole of their regimen remain the same. It has further been demonstrated that the body, when it departs from its natural and well-proportioned state, requires the assistance appropriate to it in the very respect in which it has departed and been altered: when dried, it needs to be moistened; when moistened, to be dried; when heated, to be cooled; when cooled, to be heated. When, therefore, through some concurrence of circumstances, of which he himself will give examples, it happens that certain small veins are dried in any part of the body whatever, these draw to themselves the moistures from the neighbouring parts.

If, then, the moistures carried into the dried veins, just as they have a moist nature in their consistency, so also have a moistening power, the part recovers its natural good mixture; but if the moisture is pungent in quality and drying in power, the body is set ablaze, just as if one of us ourselves, having become thirsty, were to gulp down greedily either unmixed wine treated with sea-water or 736 salty water. I myself, at any rate, know that once, having become thirsty from a summer journey on foot, and then having drunk a single cup of old wine that was a little too strongly mixed, I rather increased my thirst by it than stopped it. Just as we, then, although we have reason presiding over our appetites, sometimes through greater carelessness, sometimes through greater rashness, and sometimes because something better was not at hand, have been compelled to resort to one of the salty and pungent drinks, so too the attractive faculty in the veins continually draws in the moisture from the neighbouring parts, without discriminating what sort of thing its substance is; for it does not possess reason so as to consider anything about what is better, but just as children and grazing animals, when thirsty, take whatever liquid happens to be at hand, in the same way does that faculty too. If, then, this condition arises in some one part of the body, there will be in that part alone an erysipelas-like affection.

The biting of the parts about the belly, however, is due to the acridity of the ichors flowing together into it; 741 and the stools are in accordance with the humour that is in excess. He called them very watery, indicating that they have not been concocted at all; for concoction draws everything together and thickens it. Sleeplessness befalls those who are so affected because of the dryness; for it has been shown that moisture beyond due measure produces states of heavy sleep (kataphorai), whereas great dryness produces sleeplessness. There is added, moreover, distress arising from the other symptoms, which becomes a cause of the sleeplessness. And we have learned that delirium arises both through bile running up to the head and through dryness and heat of the mixture. In acute fevers the boiling part of the blood is borne to the head; 749 so when nature, having broken open the veins, pours this out together with the vapours that have been collected, it masters the rest more readily; and by the same reasoning, when through the sweats too it pours out the boiling ichors, it cures the disease—provided, that is, that they supervene when the disease has been concocted. For this has already been said many times, both in certain other exegetical commentaries and in those On Crises. Just as, then, in the first part of this book, the part agreed by all to be genuine, he took up the indicator drawn from the concoction of the disease as useful for regimen, so now too for prediction; he did not write the actual name of concoction, but he wrote its surest sign in the urines. The best urine, then, is that which has a white and smooth sediment, as has been shown in the Prognostic; yet you will not expect it always to appear, but often a good suspended matter (enaeorema), appearing in addition to the natural colour and consistency, will suffice you for the hope of recovery.

For which reason too the most authoritative remedy for causus will seem to have been omitted, namely the drinking of cold water, by which we have throughout treated causus, no one having died to whom we gave cold water at the proper moment—a matter about which I went through briefly in the exegesis of the former part of this book, and at greater length in other commentaries and treatises. I find that the ancient Greeks sometimes apply the name 'genus' also to things that are spoken of homonymously, whereas properly it belongs to things that have one signification but which, through the division made in accordance with it, arrive at several differentiae; in which case we are often accustomed to say that the generic differentiae of such-and-such a thing are 754 two or three or four or as many as is possible. But since the account is judged by the conception, we must consider whether we possess a conception of the causus fever that is agreed upon in the same way as that of man and ox and horse; and since the discussion is likely to run out to a length greater than befits a commentary, we shall hasten to compress it, as we do the others too, into a brief summary, making this the starting point of the discussion.

Perhaps, then, it will seem to someone that it suffices to posit only two indications 765 for phlebotomy, the magnitude of the disease and the strength of the faculty; for indeed the old man does not tolerate phlebotomy not because of his many years in and of themselves, but because of the weakness of his faculty. But children, though they are strong in their vital faculty, nevertheless do not themselves endure phlebotomy either; for their substance is readily dispersed, on account of both the moistness and the heat of their temperament; they therefore have no need of phlebotomy, since they possess as something innate the evacuation that arises from their temperament. For these reasons, then, it does not suffice for the magnitude of the disease and the strength of the faculty to be the indications for phlebotomy, but it is better to add also the age of those in their prime. However, what stands at the beginning of the passage is worth examining, how it is stated: "you will phlebotomize the acute affections"; and how it is that he did not mention the chronic ones. For indeed all the fiery and hot diseases are signified by it: erysipelata, herpetes, anthrakes, and the very things properly named 770 phlegmonai. But all the more recent physicians apply the name which was formerly common to all of them to one single kind of inflamed bodies, and call by it only that swelling which is resistant and painful, together with much heat. And since there are also other swellings contrary to nature, such as the scirrhus and what is called oedema by the more recent physicians (for this too was formerly a common name for all swellings contrary to nature, and furthermore also for inflation with pneuma), we have spoken elsewhere, in a single book, about swellings contrary to nature; but in the present discussion, just as with the other matters, this too has been stated under its main heads. Scirrhus is the swelling that is resistant and painless; and pneumatosis comes about in two ways, flatulent pneuma being collected either in certain perceptible cavities or in ones discernible by reason. At any rate, some have sometimes cut into swellings contrary to nature in muscles, expecting to find pus in the depth, and then found nothing other than pneuma scattered in small portions throughout the whole flesh.

And indeed those who cut in this way sometimes 771 found only clots, or a viscous or mucus-like fluid. But in such cases the swelling was located at the clot or the mucus, the flesh appearing to be in its usual state; whereas the pneuma is dispersed in small portions throughout the flesh itself. Accordingly, in the passage before us in the text, the "inflamed hypochondria" seem to me not to have been spoken of in the sense customary for Hippocrates. For what meaning will the phrase added to it, "not by interception of winds," have, when the flame-like heat in the hypochondria, whether it is accompanied by pneuma or not, carries the same indication? Nor, however, does he seem to have spoken in such a way that it is said of a conjunction of burning heat and interception of winds occurring together, which is false; for the interception of pneuma never brings on a flame-like condition in the hypochondrium. The writer of these words, then, seems to call "inflamed hypochondria" those that are raised up into a swelling. Following these he mentioned tension of the diaphragm, and then the forward-straining (πρότασις) of winds.

774 In commenting on 'one should purge and move what is concocted' I have already explained this aphorism, with reference to the same symptoms as here too. He rightly judges that one should come first to phlebotomy, whenever certain bad humours flow together and collect in some part—which, as I said, is called 'being gathered up' (συστρέφεσθαι) in that part. But the clause at the end of the statement written above some people make indistinguishable in sense, writing the word 'purging' incorrectly with regard to its ending (μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν), the author having said that phlebotomy 'with purging' (μετὰ φαρμακείαν) requires safety and moderation—they making the so-called accusative case in place of the genitive. For in the whole statement this is the very thing being advised: to come to phlebotomy first, and then next to purging, not the reverse, as they write it, that purging is taken up first and then in this way one comes to phlebotomy. He added to the statement the words, 'if this should happen to someone in health without a prophasis or any other strong cause', calling 'prophasis' the manifest cause, as if someone wrestling or competing in the pankration were brought into danger of being strangled from the encircling of the forearms; and 'another strong cause' such as arises in those who are struck out of their senses through 776 very great fear or grief. Distinguishing the loss of voice set forth in the statement from such losses of voice, he for this reason added, 'if it happens to someone in health'. 'One must therefore let blood from the right upper arm, from the inner vein, and remove blood, reckoning the greater and the lesser amount according to the habit of body and the age.' Most quickly and most abundantly does this vein empty the body from the most authoritative parts, and for this reason one has recourse to it in the most acute diseases. 'And remove blood, reckoning the greater and the lesser amount according to the habit of body and the age.'

Earlier, when he was stating the aims of 777 phlebotomy, he left out the habit of the body, whereas now he has not mentioned the faculty. Some think that the term "habit" has been used in place of the term "faculty", both being said of one and the same thing; but they suppose wrongly. For we use "habit" with reference to the constitution of the body, when one person is soft and another hard; whereas the strength of the faculty we recognise by the vehemence of the activities. So these are two aims, having the common indication for evacuating from what is common to them, but differing from one another, just as indeed they differ also from the indication from age. It is possible, however, to refer age rather to the habit of the body, not to the faculty; for children, on account of the softness of their habit, are indeed easily dissipated, and the elderly, on account of dryness and coldness, are dissipated with difficulty. And one can say that these three aims of phlebotomy suffice, since we take the indication from the magnitude of the affection being treated, from the habit, and from the faculty; but it has been said earlier that one must also examine the ambient air, how it stands in respect of its mixture.

The motion of pains is accustomed to set in motion an influx of humours toward the part that has the pain. When, 781 therefore, the body is more cacochymous, influxes of black bile and of other pungent humours occur, on account of which the patient suffers pain still more and the inner parts are bitten; and by the humours mentioned the veins in the affected part are distressed, being bitten, and this very thing becomes the cause of another, contrary condition (ἑτέρου... αἴτιον ἐναντίον). For when the suffering part has been filled by such fluxes, the blood itself is first corrupted, and the vessels are filled up, and this prevents all the passages of the pneumata through it; for this at least he himself showed clearly when he said, 'the pneumata not being able to travel their natural paths in it', which a little earlier he called 'interception of the pneumata'.

The motion of pains is wont to set in motion an afflux of fluids to the part that has the pain. When, 781 therefore, the body is in a more cacochymous condition, influxes of black bile and of other acrid humours take place, on account of which the patient is in still greater pain and the internal parts are bitten. And by the humours mentioned the veins in the affected part are distressed as they are bitten, and this very thing becomes the cause of another, contrary, effect. For when the suffering part has been filled by such fluxes, first the blood itself is corrupted, and the vessels are filled up, and this obstructs all the passages of the pneumata in it. For he himself made this clear when he said 'the pneumata not being able to travel their natural paths in it', which a little earlier he called interception of the pneumata.

But when the blood comes to a standstill, and with it, evidently, the pneuma, there arise chillings, darkenings of vision, losses of voice, heaviness of the head and spasms; and upon these follow also paraplexiae and epilepsies, whenever the fluxes fall upon the places surrounding the veins that have been filled. By "places" he has evidently meant the parts of the body which he himself added in writing, heart and liver and the vein, 782 namely the one that joins the aforesaid viscera, which was later named the hollow vein (vena cava) by the physicians, since it is the widest of the veins in the body of the animal. Reasonably, then, the blood in these places, because the veins have been filled, does not permit the pneuma to pass through, but congeals as in a dead body. This the author himself also made clear: "and, the pneumata being unable to pass through, it is dried up"; though it would have been more proper to say "it is somewhat congealed". For indeed both things that are dried and things that are chilled congeal; but in the present case it is not through being dried that the blood congeals, together with the bad humours that have flowed into it. For when these are passing out, they render the whole blood at once unputrefied and fluid in its natural state; but when they have come to a standstill and have cast off the innate heat and are being extinguished, the congealing of the blood comes about as in a dead body. Accordingly, when those who are ill in this way have been phlebotomised, the blood is seen to be cold and thick and to flow out of the veins only with difficulty, precisely because of this chilling.

The author himself also indicated this: 'and since the pneumata are unable to pass through, it is dried up'; but it would have been more proper to say 'it is partly congealed'. For indeed both things that are being dried and things that are being cooled congeal; but in the present case the blood, and the bad humours that have flowed into it, do not congeal through being dried. "And, restoring [the patient] and observing the crises, purge upwards if he is not relieved; and the lower belly, if it does not pass [its contents], [purge] with a clyster; give boiled ass's milk, and let him drink not less than twelve kotylai; and if his strength allows, more, sixteen." After the evacuation by phlebotomy he bids one restore and strengthen the person, so that, if he appears not at all relieved, he may be brought to the purgation through the upper parts, that is, the one through vomiting. He has omitted to name the purgative drug, nor indeed did he indicate it by making a selection of it; for it is quite clear that, looking to the magnitude of the disease and the strength of the faculty, we shall give either white hellebore or one of the other things that provoke vomiting. What has been said about the lower belly is evident; and do not be surprised at the quantity of the milk, for this was customary with all the ancients.

But it has also been said that in those so disposed the artery (windpipe) 795 is ulcerated, evidently because of the acridity of the humour. And he said that the lung, being deprived [of the external breath], is set on fire, connecting his statement with a true doctrine; for it has been demonstrated in On the Use of Respiration that upon deprivation of respiration the animal perishes not through a deficiency of the substance, but because the innate heat loses its cooling and fanning. Reasonably, then, being in the grip of disproportion, it sets the lung on fire. Accordingly he says that this form of kynanche is more dangerous and less escapable than the former, both on account of what has been said before and because the season is summer and autumn, and because it supervenes upon more acrid humours. Better, therefore, is the reading with the conjunction 'and' than that without the conjunction 'and'; for, beyond what was said before, it indicates in addition that the second form of synanche is more grievous both on account of the season in which it occurs and on account of the humour by which [it is produced]; so one must not write simply that it is more dangerous and less escapable because of the season.

And he said that the lung, being deprived, is burned up, joining his account to a true doctrine. For it has been shown in the work On the Use of Breathing that, when breathing is taken away, the animal perishes not through a deficiency of the substance, but because the innate heat loses its cooling and fanning. Reasonably, then, the innate heat, being in a state of disproportion, burns up the lung. This form of kynanchē, therefore, he says is more dangerous and more inescapable than the former, both because of what was said before and because the season is summer and autumn, and because it arises from more acrid humours. The reading with the conjunction 'and' is therefore better than the reading without the conjunction 'and'. For, in addition to what was said before, the 'and' also indicates that it is both because of the season in which it occurs and because of the humour by which it is produced that the second form of synanchē is more severe. Nature therefore requires, just as when the nourishment has been swallowed down into the stomach, rest from the other motions, so that it may be at leisure for the activity concerned with concoction alone, and some aid from outside whenever at some time it becomes weaker; in the same manner, in the case of the concoction of the humours in the veins, it requires rest 811 before the second heat, from being heated and cooled or dried and moistened, each of these obviously occurring at one time or another. When 823 any of these things is present in the hypochondrium, above all one should loosen the belly with clysters; and let him drink warm boiled melikraton. He says that one must first keep watch over the first 824 day, on which he bids us recognize the cause of the disease; for the 'from what' and the 'when' make clear what the disease is. He bids us inquire first how the head is, then the hypochondria and the sides: as to the hypochondrium, whether there is any pain, or whether it is drawn up (ἐξήρτηται), or has some crookedness (σκολιότητα), that is, irregularity—which he wrote in the Prognostic in these words, 'if the right and the left sides are irregularly disposed'; or whether it has satiety, he says, and this seems to me to be repletion with food. He also requires one to ask the other things in the passage that follows; and then he bids, when the hypochondria are affected, to loosen the belly with clysters, and to drink warm boiled melikraton. Having said these things without qualification, he writes next: one must also observe closely what happens at the risings-up [from bed], whether he faints and whether, he says, ease of breathing is upon him; and this is set in opposition to the one who faints. He also requires one to look at the stool, whether it is black or clean and faultless, such as that of the healthy, just as also whether the fever has a further exacerbation on the third day.

He says that one must first keep watch over the first 824 day, on which he bids us recognise the cause of the disease; for the 'from what' and the 'when' make plain what the disease actually is. He bids us inquire first how the head is, then the hypochondria and the sides: of the hypochondrium, whether there is some pain, or whether it is drawn up, or has some crookedness, that is, unevenness. This he wrote in the Prognostic in these words: 'if it is unevenly disposed on the right and on the left.' 'Or whether it has satiety,' he says; and this seems to me to be the filling with foods. He thinks fit to ask about the other things too, in connection with the passage that follows; and then he bids, when the hypochondria are affected, to loosen the belly with clysters, and to drink hot, boiled-down melicrat. Having said this without qualification, he writes next: 'one must also observe what happens at the risings, whether he faints, and whether,' he says, 'ease of breath possesses him'; this is the opposite of the fainting patient. He thinks fit to look also at the evacuation, whether it is black or clean and faultless, such as that of healthy people, just as also whether the fever has a further exacerbation on the third day.

But when he does not respond to the suppository, and there is present, in respect of the breath, 826 ease, if, when he has got up onto the stool, or right there in the bed, fainting (ἀψυχίη) is present—when these things are present in the male or the female patient at the beginning, expect that delirium will come. The sense of this passage is confused. For the statement that, when the suppository accomplishes nothing but the patient seems to be bearing things easily, if indeed he also faints when getting up, one should expect delirium, seems to me to be badly said, since neither experience nor reasoning bears witness to it. For to faint after sudden evacuations is dangerous, just as it is also to become voiceless and nauseous; and it is not good either to sweat about the face and the head alone. Just as these, then, are many and bad symptoms, so too are the others written in the Prognostic; and someone, by weaving them together with one another, can seem to be teaching something newer. And if somewhere he also mixes an unclear expression into his account, like a riddle, he will seem to the many to be wiser on this account as well, for they marvel at what they do not understand. But by a man who has learned to distinguish the supervening features from the pathognomonic concurrence, the account will be detected as intricate, but useless. For the pathognomonic concurrence indicates the kind of the disease, whereas the supervening symptoms indicate its mildness and its malignancy.

And one who has learned the force of each of these symptoms must reckon up and compare with one another the things that appear; and if the bad ones appear stronger and more numerous than the good, 832 one must recognise that the person is in danger; but if the good ones should be stronger and more numerous than the bad, one may hold a fair expectation for the patient. And this is what Hippocrates himself requires you to do: at any rate, in the Prognostic he taught the force of each of all the symptoms and signs taken singly, and at the end of that treatise he says: "He who is going to foretell correctly those who will survive and those who will die, and those in whom the disease is going to persist for more days and those in whom for fewer, must learn all the signs thoroughly and judge by reckoning up their forces in relation to one another, as has been described." He requires one, by reckoning up the forces of the signs, to foreknow from them what is going to result. Where, then, good signs are mixed with bad ones that are in some way equal to them in force, it requires a man who is trained and has observed these things many times in practice; but where they are either all bad, as in the present case, or all good, what is going to happen is evident to everyone.

But since the sign is always bad, and somewhat more so in summer and in the first part of autumn, 843 it turns out that its force is intensified; for in these days yellow bile abounds and the surrounding air is hot, so that on both accounts the blood ought to flow easily. Therefore the magnitude of the cause is indicated on account of which it is prevented from flowing, which he says is the tension (συντονία), perhaps naming the condensation in this way. However, the statement that those in this condition need treatment in respect of the veins as yet teaches nothing, before he says what treatment he means; yet he did not say it, but wrote only a first prediction, that appearances of thin urines occur on the following day — though they necessarily appear unconcocted not only on this day but also on the days before it. And he says that convulsion and delirium will occur when the patient is thus in the prime of his age; further, in addition to these, he mentions also his being given to gymnastic exercise and his good fleshiness and his temperament (for 'melancholic' is the name of a temperament), and moreover he says that from drinking he has trembling hands.

That those in this condition need treatment in respect of the veins, however, teaches nothing as yet, until he says what treatment he means. Yet he did not say it; instead he first wrote only a prediction, that appearances of thin urine occur on the following day, although these necessarily appear unconcocted not on this day alone but also on the days before it. He also says that convulsion and derangement will occur if the patient is in this way in the prime of his age. They differ from one another in that the abscession brings on the crisis itself and frees the patient from all troubles, whereas the metastasis contains the beginning of other paroxysms and pains, so that the part of the body into which the metastasis of the offending humours has taken place needs again another period of time for concoction; wherefore he also added, 'and when these have been concocted, the discharges of sputa occur, or of thick urines, smooth, white', teaching the signs that the metastasis has been concocted, from the concocted sputa and urines.

And moreover, at the beginning of the passage as well, after 'they are violently drawn back forwards', he then says 'the tendons, the tail ones (οὐρωδέων), being dried, which, being thicker, hold the spine together'. He calls by this name those that reach as far as the οὐραῖον, and they name as οὐραῖον the end of the bone. But if he wishes to indicate that both parts are stretched, both in front and behind, it is possible for a tetanus to be intensified, as he said a little before, 'and in tetanus of the loin'. Nor is it reliably, either, that he foreknows the easing of the affections from the concoction of the urine. For in a feverish disease the lack of concoction is shown clearly through the urine, but for affections in the muscles the indication given by the urine is not reliable.

If one must judge each single one of the things eaten by experience, garlic would not rightly be said to be flatulent, nor to bring to those who have eaten it a sensation of greater heat than in the case of onion, either in any other part of the body or in the 872 thorax; and in the same way not a sensation of nausea either, and especially if one takes it after having first boiled it briefly. Most foods heat when the body is plethoric, but when it has been previously evacuated they dry quite considerably. The author of the book has therefore erred in making his statement without a distinction; for it would have been better to draw the distinction, as has been said, whereas as it is he made his declaration about garlic speaking without qualification. It would have been better to say that it dries and heats and is non-flatulent; for it is not the custom to make declarations about an undistinguished case. And one should understand in addition 'whenever it is given at the right moment', which means 'to a body that has been prepared beforehand'; and a body is prepared beforehand by being neither plethoric nor cacochymous. So neither is he right in saying that heaviness of the head is produced by it; for if one first evacuates the body and then administers garlic, one will cure heaviness both of the head and of every other part. And I am amazed how, having first said about it the things he has gone through up to this point, he says next: 'but it is best to eat it either when one is about to go to a drinking-party or when one is drunk.'

This, he says, and in addition 878 the juice of the plant, produces dry cholera in the inexperienced, that is, in those unaccustomed to it; and what this is he himself will teach a little later, writing thus: 'In dry cholera the belly is inflated and there are rumblings in it.' For just as moist cholera arises from pungent humours generated out of the corruption of the foods that have been eaten, so the dry arises from pungent flatulent pneuma; wherefore also the sinewy bodies adjoining the 886 belly, being bitten and stretched, produce pain. But since these pneumata are able sometimes to be retained and sometimes to pass through, I am not able to say that it is on account of the retained pneumata that dry cholera is engendered; for it would have been more plausible to give this name to those that pass out. Watch over such a patient so that he does not vomit, but that the bowel passes downward. It is beneficial also for such a one to sleep; and to drink wine that is thin and old and rather unmixed; and give oil, so that there may be quiet and the bowel may pass and it is resolved; and let them abstain from food and from everything else. 887 To administer a clyster as quickly as possible and to prevent vomiting are precepts common to all things contained in the belly contrary to nature which we are eager to have excreted downward; and in the same way also the clystering with a warm clyster, for what is warm is provocative, just as what is cold is repellent. But that the clyster be oily is a remedy proper to the dry [cholera], because it is also opposite in its power, moistening the dryness and soothing the biting. To the same aims also belongs the warming and soothing by means of water and by means of oil, fomenting him in the tub. "It is beneficial also for such a person to sleep." It is unclear whether he bids him sleep while being fomented in the tub, or also apart from it; but to one considering the matter in and of itself it is evident that it is most beneficial for all those [suffering] from lack of concoction. "And to drink wine that is thin and old and more undiluted." Wine he gives as contributing to concoction; thin, so that it may not remain in the stomach; old and more undiluted for the sake of warming more; for all wine warms the bodily condition, but old wine more so.

If the belly is moist and bile passes downward, and there are gripings 889 and vomitings and chokings, for these it is best to keep still, and to drink melikraton and vomit it up. It will, then, be brought down moderately by the melikraton, and concocted by the rest. Often, however, in such dispositions one who gives aid in a combative manner purges out the bad humour (kakochymia) all at once with a strong drug, having first additionally considered the strength and the habit of body of the sick person, and the season, and the age, and the prevailing state (katastasis). It is the greatest part of dietetics to observe and to keep watch, as in acute so also in long illnesses, over both the intensifications of the fevers and the 899 remissions, so as to preserve the right moments—when one must not administer food, and to know securely when one must administer it; and further, when they are farthest removed from the intensification. He says that the greatest thing in the dietetic art is to recognise the particular right moment for nourishment; he himself, then, states one indicator: that the moment at which one must give nourishment is farthest removed from the intensification; and by 'intensification' he would be meaning the beginning of the paroxysm. This seems to be true not only in the case of chronic diseases but also in acute ones; why, then, did he add 'in long illnesses'? Because in these the indicator is more evident, or perhaps even the only one. For in acute diseases it was a sufficient sign of the right moment for nourishment that the heat had come down to the feet, yet in chronic diseases one must certainly not give nourishment in this way, but it is fitting to wait for the best part of the remission; for in acute diseases it is not possible to wait, out of fear of the intensification that is going to come shortly.

But it appears, if one examines this point by itself, without connecting it with the discovery in the particular case of the right moment for nourishment, that the precept about nourishment is untimely and worth nothing.

902 Let us see, then, whom from the beginning he forbids us to purge. Those with headache, he says, from gymnastic exercises or some other untimely exertion. Taking it concisely, then, understand it thus: do not purge those who have become subject to headache from untimely exertions. Untimely exertions are in every case those which the disposition of the body present at that time is unable to bear. I shall now remind you of a matter useful for many purposes, which I think you should keep in mind throughout: when our body partakes of a preparation (for disease) that is close to being completed, something approaching from outside exposes its disposition, kindling a fever or stirring up headache or catarrh or cough, or some other such thing; and then, as a consequence of this, in continuity with the preparation of the morbid disposition, they fall dangerously ill, though it was not the running that generated the disease, nor the violent motion in general, just as it was not the intemperance or the chilling or any other of such things.

For none of them is capable, by its own nature, of producing severe weakness; rather, if a fever should arise from any one of them, such a fever belongs to those called ephemeral, and if 903 it is some other symptom, it will often be of short duration. And this very thing, as I said, is because of the disposition of the body: each of such things becomes not the cause of the disease but its occasion. For one would most properly name such causes occasions, not simply evident ones, as they themselves are often accustomed to call them, whenever a clear injury arises in the body from one of the evident causes; for when no other morbid disposition underlies, neither will any disease worth mentioning follow, and of the injury that comes about in the body, what produced it is the cause. Know, therefore, that his present discourse has been concerned with causes of this kind, which do not harm the body in their own right; and the main heading of them is, one and first, the exertions, which in their particulars are of many kinds—runs and wrestlings and pancration, sexual intercourse, rubbings, heat-burning, chilling, sleeplessness, fits of anger, griefs, fears.

For none of them is capable, by its own nature, of producing a severe illness; but whether a fever should arise from one of them (such a fever is of the kind called ephemeral), or 903 some other symptom, it will often be short-lived. Then about the affections arising from the womb (hysterical affections), then about mekonion, then next a hydragogue drug, then one that expels faeces, then for those with complaints of the seat (anus) and for the dropsical he gives [a remedy] made through mekonion and 919 itria (sesame-cakes).
